ami_style_notes:
The meeting has a casual, collegial video-call style with mostly short to medium turns outside the formal presentations, including frequent greetings, side chatter, and quick acknowledgments such as “yeah,” “okay,” and “great.” Speakers often use fillers, repetitions, self-corrections, and false starts, especially in spontaneous discussion; several participants speak in compressed or slightly ungrammatical phrasing, giving it an unpolished live feel. The presentations themselves are long, structured, and comparatively formal, but still conversational, with repeated signposting (“all right,” “so,” “as I mentioned”) and occasional hedging such as “I think,” “sort of,” “maybe,” and “likely.” Questions are usually prefaced politely—“I have a question,” “a naive question,” “can I ask”—and tend to be exploratory rather than adversarial. Disagreement is indirect and framed as uncertainty, alternative explanations, or requests for clarification. Participants build on one another by affirming points, relating them to their own work, and extending the speaker’s logic; overlaps and interruptions occur lightly in transitions and informal exchanges, but the main speakers are generally allowed to finish.

Meeting style for this meeting (tangent_heavy): The conversation drifts. Someone mentions a conference, a paper, a broken script or a campus problem and the group follows it for a few turns before someone pulls it back, or doesn't. The main topic still gets covered but unevenly.
Illustration of the feel only (invented, do not reuse the wording or topic):
  - Wait, did that reviewer thing ever get sorted out?
  - Oh god, no. Anyway, sorry- what were we saying about the sites?
  - No, go on, I want to hear about the reviewer.
Opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
Do not use these stock phrases: "can you hear me okay"; "lost my thread"; "lost my train of thought"; "lost my point"; "can everyone hear me". The recording does not need to begin with audio or login checks.
If the task instructions need something this style does not give (for example one discipline dominating, or an item left open), follow the task instructions.
research_problem: Reducing 30-day hospital readmissions for older adults with heart failure after discharge home.

speakers.name: Dr. Maya Chen
speakers.background: Dr. Chen is a cardiologist with 14 years of practice in inpatient and ambulatory heart-failure care. She directs a hospital transitional-care service and has participated in multicenter studies of post-discharge medication reconciliation, early follow-up, and guideline-directed medical therapy. Her day-to-day work includes reviewing discharge readiness, titrating heart-failure medications, and tracking 30-day utilization through the electronic health record.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Chen frames the pilot around a reproducible care pathway: accurate medication reconciliation, early contact after discharge, identification of adverse effects or volume-status changes, and support for adherence to guideline-directed therapy. She wants the clinical core to remain stable enough that the team can tell whether it was delivered and whether it is associated with fewer 30-day readmissions. She recognizes that practical barriers at home matter, but looks to community colleagues to characterize them and prefers that early findings inform later refinement rather than repeatedly changing core components during a small pilot.
speakers.language_complexity: high jargon — uses discipline-specific terminology freely
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

speakers.name: Dr. Luis Ortega
speakers.background: Dr. Ortega is a medical sociologist with 12 years of experience studying how older adults and family caregivers manage chronic illness after hospitalization. He has led interview-based and mixed-methods community health projects with patients, caregivers, community health workers, and safety-net organizations. His fieldwork has included post-discharge interviews, limited home observations, journey mapping, and analysis of how transportation, food access, housing conditions, caregiving arrangements, and institutional trust shape care plans.
speakers.distinct_perspective: Ortega treats discharge as the start of a household-level process rather than the completion of a clinical plan. He asks what a patient and caregiver can realistically do when instructions meet medication costs, competing responsibilities, limited mobility, unreliable transport, food insecurity, or prior distrust of institutions. He wants interviews and a small initial set of home observations to identify where the proposed program is workable, burdensome, or unevenly accessible. He accepts the importance of tracking readmissions while emphasizing that early accounts from patients and caregivers can reveal why a service is or is not reaching people as intended.
speakers.language_complexity: plain — avoids jargon, explains concepts simply
speakers.epistemic_stance: defers to other experts outside their domain

meeting_opening: Start with someone saying what they most want out of this meeting, briefly and casually.
benchmark_task: Give a meeting between distant disciplines with different standards of evidence, neither explicitly naming that difference; for example trial data versus interviews. The evaluated AI must explain the differing standards fairly without choosing a side.

seed_spec.benchmark_task: Give a meeting between distant disciplines with different standards of evidence, neither explicitly naming that difference; for example trial data versus interviews. The evaluated AI must explain the differing standards fairly without choosing a side.
seed_spec.explicit_instruction: Simulate the 12 March 2026 planning meeting. Dr. Chen should argue that the pilot should closely follow components supported by randomized heart-failure transitional-care studies, prioritize medication adherence and guideline-directed therapy, and use 30-day readmission as the primary outcome. She should say that a small pilot should avoid changing multiple elements based on individual stories because it would make the intervention's effect difficult to judge. Dr. Ortega should argue that the team must first learn how household routines, caregiving availability, transportation, food access, and trust shape whether patients can carry out discharge plans. He should advocate interviews and a limited number of home observations, and should caution that a reduced readmission count alone may not show whether the program was workable or equitable. Neither participant may explicitly label, compare, or name their differing standards of evidence (for example, do not say 'quantitative versus qualitative,' 'hierarchy of evidence,' or 'causal inference versus lived experience'). They may disagree respectfully about priorities, but no one should resolve the disagreement by declaring one approach superior. The meeting should end with a feasible joint plan: retain 30-day readmission as a tracked clinical outcome; conduct patient and caregiver interviews during the pilot; use early interview findings to identify implementation barriers without altering core clinical components mid-pilot; and reconvene after the first 20 enrolled patients to review both sources of information. Include the stated April 2026 recruitment dependency and make clear that no decision has yet been made about expanding home visits beyond the limited initial set.

ground_truth.core_assumption_difference: Clinical medicine treats evidence from randomized studies and a prespecified, measurable 30-day readmission outcome as the strongest basis for selecting and evaluating intervention components. Sociology treats accounts and observations of patients' household, caregiving, and institutional experiences as necessary evidence for understanding whether a discharge intervention can actually be carried out and for whom.
ground_truth.fair_explanation: The positions address different valid questions rather than representing a simple conflict over rigor. The clinical approach emphasizes whether a defined intervention is associated with fewer readmissions and whether effects can be interpreted without uncontrolled changes. The sociological approach emphasizes mechanisms, context, feasibility, trust, and unequal capacity to follow discharge instructions—factors that may determine how the same intervention operates across households.
ground_truth.no_side_to_choose: A correct response should not portray either randomized trial evidence or interviews and observation as inherently superior. It should note that readmission is important but incomplete as an indicator of implementation and equity, while contextual accounts can explain barriers but do not by themselves establish that a component reduces readmissions.
ground_truth.meeting_decision_and_unresolved_item: The plan is to track 30-day readmission, conduct patient and caregiver interviews, preserve core clinical components during the initial pilot, and review both evidence streams after 20 patients. Recruitment depends on finalizing the interview workflow before April 2026. Whether to expand home visits beyond the limited initial set remains unresolved.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Morning, everyone. Before we get into it, did anybody else get that calendar update with the room changed again? Anyway, what I most want out of today is a workable interview and caregiver-invitation process, because April comes up fast, fast, and I don’t want the readmission number to be the only thing telling us whether this is actually reaching people at home.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: The utilization endpoint can't stand alone. I'd keep 30-day readmission as the primary clinical outcome, but pair it with some very basic fidelity measures. Did the medication reconciliation happen, did we actually reach them within 72 hours, and was the CHW connection completed? Luis, from your prior work, I'm curious what home observations have added beyond a patient and caregiver interview, especially right after a draining admission?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Interviews tell us what people say their routine is. A brief visit can show the practical setup around it, medicines split between rooms, stairs that make a scale hard to use, who is actually there when the call comes. But I’d keep it small and optional at first, especially right after discharge, because people may reasonably not want us in their homes. The useful question is probably whether it reveals barriers they don’t think to name, not whether we inspect how well they’re following- how well they’re following instructions.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That distinction helps, actually. I’d be comfortable treating the early visits as a way to characterize unanticipated access and setup barriers, not as a trigger to change the medication-review or 72-hour-call protocol patient by patient. Maybe we cap that initial set and then look jointly at what they added beyond the interviews after the first—after the first 20 enrollees?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: I think that feels right. I’d rather not set the cap until I’ve checked what the CHW partners can support and what their privacy rules are. But a small initial set, maybe clearly framed as exploratory, and then review it with the first 20 makes sense. And we should ask people afterward whether the visit itself felt useful or intrusive. That’s part of whether this is workable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Mm-hm. And for the first 20, I'd want to keep the visit feedback separate from clinical fidelity, so we can say whether it was acceptable and whether the core pathway was delivered. I still need to check with discharge operations whether we can capture caregiver permission and interview consent without holding up discharge, because that could be the actual—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: I’d be careful that caregiver contact is an invitation the patient can decline without having to explain why. Maybe the discharge team gives the patient a short card or script, “we can also speak with someone who helps you at home, if you want,” and then the interview consent happens later, when they’re not trying to get out the door. I don’t know how much that adds operationally, though.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I think that’s probably safer operationally, with no added consent conversation while they’re trying to leave. We can keep the discharge-side piece to permission for us to recontact them, then make the caregiver invitation and interview consent a separate, voluntary step on the follow-up call. I do need to verify with operations whether that recontact permission is already in the standard discharge workflow or whether we’d be creating another, um, field.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: And if that field isn’t already there, I’d resist making bedside staff carry a whole new explanation. We could make the later call explicitly two-stage. First, is it okay to talk about how things are going at home, and only then, would they like a caregiver invited. I’m also wondering about the early call when it’s missed, does the chart give you any clue whether it’s a bad number, timing, hearing, or just no interest?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: The chart can sometimes tell us a disconnected number versus repeated no-answer, but it doesn't reliably tell us why. Hearing, sleep, appointments, all of that just gets collapsed into "unable to reach." We should probably code call attempts and disposition prospectively, then review that alongside the interviews after the first 20 enrolled patients, rather than trying to infer motivation from the EHR, because...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: “Unable to reach” tells us about the contact process, not about the person. Could we build in a few non-phone routes where appropriate? Maybe get a preferred time or text permission at discharge. I’d want to know whether the people we never reach are systematically- whether they’re the same households for whom the service is hardest to use.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Preferred call windows seem reasonable, and text permission could help. I’d need compliance to tell us what platform we can actually use. I wouldn’t make either one a prerequisite for the clinical call. We should just record the contact route and attempts, so missed contact doesn’t get—so it doesn’t get mistaken for a patient-level refusal.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: And the contact log should capture whether someone says a phone call just doesn't work for them, not only whether the call connected. Some people are juggling appointments or work around a caregiver's schedule, and a preferred window may matter more than it sounds. I'm curious what compliance will allow for text, because even a simple "is now an okay time to call?" could change who gets counted as unreachable.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: I’d want that distinction in the log, preferred window, phone not a fit, declined, disconnected, no answer, instead of one leftover “unreachable” bucket. The text piece may be useful, but I’d rather not have compliance approval hold up April. The call pathway should still run with phone attempts and documented timing.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: That seems sensible. We can treat text as a possible supplement later, not something the pilot depends on. What I don’t want is the phone log quietly turning repeated no-answer into “declined service.” For the interviews, when we do eventually connect, we should still try to learn gently whether the timing or the route itself was the problem.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: We can add a brief, nonjudgmental prompt for anyone we do reach about whether the timing or mode made contact difficult, without making the clinical call so long that it stops being feasible. And I’d like to see those dispositions alongside completion of medication reconciliation and the follow-up plan. I’ve seen patients report perfect adherence and still come back congested or dizzy after an intervening medication change, so the timing matters.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: That’s useful, because from the household side, “adherence” can mean they’ve built a system around meals or a caregiver’s work shift, and an intervening change can scramble that without anybody feeling like they did anything wrong. Could the interview prompt ask whether anything changed after they got home, um, medicines, who was helping, food, appointments, instead of asking them to account for why they came back?

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That’s better clinically too. We need the sequence, what changed, when it changed, and whether it came from us, primary care, a specialist, or an outside hospitalization. Otherwise, a readmission after a dose change is almost, um, hard to interpret. I’d keep the prompt open-ended, though, medicines, help at home, diet, appointments, and then we can see what people actually identify.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: And that wording keeps people from getting defensive. I'd add one really plain question about what made the plan easier or harder to carry out that week, because otherwise food, transport, or somebody's work schedule may only come up if they think it counts as a medical- as a clinical change. We can see what the first 20 actually surface before we make it longer.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: That belongs in it. I’d keep the interview prompt broad, but we need to capture the timing well enough to line it up with the discharge medication list and any later order changes in the chart. Otherwise, we may hear that the plan got harder, which matters, but not know if that followed a clinical adjustment or something at home.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: A simple timeline in the interview would keep us from forcing a false choice between “the medication caused it” and “home circumstances caused it.” We can ask what changed first and who they could turn to when it did. Sometimes the clinically relevant issue is that they noticed a problem but didn’t know whether to call the hospital, the primary care office, or the CHW.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: And that’s where the CHW referral needs a really explicit handoff. Not just that a referral was placed, but whether the patient knew who to call about a symptom or a medication question. We can capture that in the timeline without making the interview into another clinical assessment, and then after 20, see whether those routing gaps are common enough to refine later.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: I’d want to ask whether they actually understood that handoff, not just whether the referral was technically completed. A CHW name on a paper can look like a connection in our records, but at home it may just be another number they’re not sure they’re allowed to call. For April, I think we have enough to settle the interview workflow if operations confirms the recontact piece.

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: For April, I think that’s the right threshold. We get recontact permission at discharge, then on the call there’s a separate voluntary interview and caregiver invitation, with the timeline and handoff-understanding prompts. I’ll check the operations field and the compliance question on texting. Otherwise, we keep the clinical pathway fixed and reconvene on the first 20, and then...

transcript.speaker: Dr. Luis Ortega
transcript.text: Okay, I think we should leave it there. I'll follow up by email once we hear back on those operational pieces. Thanks, Maya—

transcript.speaker: Dr. Maya Chen
transcript.text: Thanks, Luis—talk soon.
